title: Social-democratic tradition
summary: Revises the working dossier around attributed goals, institutional variation, and two bounded Swedish cases rather than treating a country as the tradition.

sources.title: The Primacy of Politics: Social Democracy and the Making of Europe’s Twentieth Century (excerpt)
sources.authorityNote: A university-press intellectual history used to establish the tradition’s historical breadth and contested effort to subordinate economic forces to democratic politics.

sources.title: The Rehn-Meidner Model in Sweden: Its Rise, Challenges and Survival
sources.authorityNote: A peer-reviewed reconstruction of the Swedish policy model, its stated goals, incomplete implementation, periodization, and internal tensions.

claims.text: Social democracy is a historically changing family of political arguments and institutions rather than a single welfare-state package.
limitations: One intellectual history cannot settle every disputed boundary or national variant.

claims.text: The Rehn–Meidner policy complex is a useful bounded expression of social-democratic institutional reasoning, not a definition of the whole tradition.
claims.rationale: The case illuminates coordinated bargaining and adjustment policy while the wider tradition includes other parties, periods, countries, and institutional combinations.
limitations: The relationship remains an editorial classification requiring human review.

conflictingEvidence.summary: The tradition has included both projects seeking gradual transition beyond capitalism and later projects accepting a durable mixed capitalist economy; the dossier must preserve rather than erase that boundary dispute.

limitations: This proposal tests a Swedish vertical slice and does not establish Nordic uniformity.
It does not classify any present-day country as an instance of the tradition.

relationships.reason: The proposed cases examine wage distribution, profit, ownership, and control as distinct outcomes.
Peak bargaining and appointed fund boards raise questions about delegated authority and contestability.
Distribution is applied without collapsing wages, wealth, ownership, and control.
Accountability makes the normative assessment of delegated authority explicit.

proposedRelationships.reason: A bounded policy episode influenced by Swedish labor and social-democratic policymaking.
A contested enacted compromise relevant to social-democratic debates over ownership and wage-earner influence.
A researched institutional combination in the Rehn–Meidner case.
The enacted fund-board design provides a distinct ownership and delegation mechanism.

duplicateCandidates.reason: This is a substantial revision proposal for the existing draft tradition, not a second tradition.

content.description: A historically varied tradition seeking to subject capitalist markets and concentrated economic power to democratic politics through combinations of social provision, worker organization, regulation, public action, and—in some variants—changes to ownership.
content.scope: A family of political and institutional arguments; excludes treating welfare spending alone, a party label, the Nordic region, or any country-period as sufficient membership.
variants: Reform traditions accepting a durable mixed capitalist economy
Democratic-socialist currents seeking gradual changes in ownership and economic authority
Nordic, continental, and other national traditions with materially different bargaining, welfare, and governance institutions
distinctions: Not synonymous with a welfare state, which can be built by several political traditions
Not synonymous with democratic socialism, though the histories and memberships overlap
Not a claim that Nordic countries form one uniform or timeless model
commonQuestions: Is social democracy the same as democratic socialism? — No; they overlap, but differ especially over whether capitalism is a durable framework or a structure to transform.
Does it require state ownership of most firms? — No; variants combine private, public, cooperative, and regulated ownership differently.
Is the Nordic model one system? — No; it is comparative shorthand covering institutions that vary by country and period.
